setup.label: Job: pawn to e5 or e6

beats.say: Fischer and Kasparov both made this their weapon. And the move that defines it looks like almost nothing: pawn to a6.
That pawn keeps White's pieces off b5, and it gets your b-pawn ready to run. Everything else stays flexible.
Think of a goalkeeper who waits for the run-up before moving. You wait for White's bishop to pick a square, then you choose your setup.
We'll build the setup, deal with five ways White tries to spoil it, learn the one punch, then watch it land in two games. You're Black, so the board is turned around.
Five fixed moves, then three jobs that depend on where White's bishop goes. Watch the list tick itself off.
White plays e4, and you answer with c5. That's the Sicilian.
White's knight comes out, and d6 keeps it off e5.
White plays d4, and you take. Nearly everyone does here, and it trades your wing pawn for White's centre pawn.
The knight takes back, and yours comes out with a hit on e4.
White guards it, and here's the move. a6. About half the players under 1800 in our Lichess sample choose it. b5 is yours now.
White's bishop goes to e3, so here's your first job. Pawn to e5 kicks the knight, and it takes the middle.
The bishop goes to e6 and watches d5. That's the square your e-pawn left behind, so keep an eye on it.
Second job, bishop to e7.
Third job, castle. That's the list.
And look where White's king just went. Now look at your a-pawn and b-pawn. They run straight at it. That's the whole plan.
Your opponent didn't read the script. Here are the five things they'll try, and you only need one answer to each.

beats.reset: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6
beats.say: One, and it's the most common, about three games in ten. Bishop to g5, pressing on your knight.
Pawn to e6 this time, not e5, because that would give up d5 with your knight under fire.
White pushes the f-pawn, and your bishop backs up the knight.
White castles long. You bring the queen and the other knight, and now you know which way to run.
Both sides push pawns. It's sharp. The engine says about plus 0.5, so this is one you'll want to drill.

beats.reset: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bg5 e6 f4
beats.say: You'll hear about this one. Queen to b6, hitting b2, is the famous Poisoned Pawn.
You really can take it, and the engine says about plus 0.2. But your queen is out on a limb, and it takes serious homework. Save it for later.

beats.reset: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6
beats.say: Two. Bishop to c4, aiming at f7. That's about one game in seven.
Pawn to e6 again, and the bishop is looking at a wall.
White castles, and your b-pawn pushes that bishop back. It gets you moving on the queenside at the same time.
Now a warning. Push on and grab e4, and it looks like a free pawn.
It isn't. The rook lands on the e-file, hitting your loose knight, and the engine jumps above plus one. Don't take it.

beats.reset: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Bc4 e6 O-O b5 Bb3
beats.say: Just do your jobs. Bishop to e7, then castle, and the engine calls it dead level.

beats.reset: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6
beats.say: Three. Bishop to d3, guarding e4. It's quiet, and it's also about one in seven.
Quiet means you get e5 with no trouble. Bishop to e2 gets the same answer.
The knight drops back, you do your jobs, and the engine calls it level.
Four. White never plays d4 at all. Bishop to c4 is about one in four here, under 1800.
Same wall. Knight out, pawn to e6. The engine says about plus 0.2.
Five. A bishop check straight away, usually to keep you out of your homework.
Just block and trade. You've got rid of a bishop, your queen is out, and the engine says about plus 0.1.

chapters.title: The punch
chapters.from: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e5 Nb3 Be6 f3 Be7 Qd2 O-O O-O-O Nbd7

beats.say: Back to the finished setup. The kings are on opposite sides, so both sides throw pawns. Yours were made ready on move five.
White's g-pawn comes at your king. Your b-pawn answers.
Now your knight's under attack, and everything in you wants to move it.
Hit back instead. Pawn to b4, and now White's knight is attacked too.
And that knight has a job. It watches d5, the hole you left behind. Chase it away, and that hole gets a lot safer.
If White takes your knight, you take the knight on c3, and that pawn hits the queen.
Queen takes, and you take back on f6. All square, and the engine says about level, and White's kingside pawns have thinned out.

beats.reset: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6 Be3 e5 Nb3 Be6 f3 Be7 Qd2 O-O O-O-O Nbd7 g4 b5 g5 b4
beats.say: A warning. It's not a forced win. The knight can just step aside to e2. Now your knight really does have to move, and the engine still gives White about half a pawn.
And your own weakness doesn't go away. Your e-pawn left a hole on d5 for good. Keep your bishop on e6 until a knight lands there and you have to deal with it.
This game is made up by us and checked by Stockfish. White's moves are all natural ones.

beats.play: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6
beats.say: The routine. Nothing to think about yet.
Bishop to e3, so pawn to e5.
Instead of dropping back, the knight jumps forward to f5. Plenty of players try this. It looks active.
So punch the middle. Your bishop is already looking at f5 as well. The engine prefers Black by about half a pawn.
White guards the knight with a pawn. It's natural, and it's the mistake. The engine goes to about minus 2.7.
Because pawn to d4 hits the knight and the bishop at once. One of them is going.
White hits back in the middle instead of saving either.
So take the bishop. You're a whole piece up.
White's bishop looks at f7. There's still a little menace here.
Don't panic. Just bring out another piece.
White kicks your knight. But your queen has been waiting behind that d-pawn.
Queen to d2, check, guarded by the pawn on e3. White should trade queens, though that loses too.
Hoping to keep queens on, the king steps to f1.
Queen to f2, and that's checkmate on move twelve. The pawn that took on e3 guards her. It's the same pawn that forked two pieces.
Also ours, also engine-checked. This time White plays it properly, and it's a real race.

beats.play: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6
beats.say: The routine again. And keep your eye on that pawn on a6.

beats.play: Be3 e5 Nb3 Be6 f3 Be7
beats.say: Bishop to e3, and you do your jobs.
White castles long, and your list is done.
White tucks the king away. You start running.
White's pawn comes at your king, and yours kicks the knight.
The knight jumps into the hole on d5, just as you were warned.
Now you deal with it. Your bishop takes, and the pawn takes back. That knight's gone, and the pawn on d5 is no threat.
And here it comes, the a-pawn from move five. It's a gamble. The engine prefers knight to b6, and says about plus 1.6 after this.
White's bishop comes out, hitting your knight. It's a slip, because pushing the g-pawn was stronger. The gamble is starting to pay.
Ignore it. Pawn to a4 hits the knight on b3.
And White ignores that, and hits your knight on f6. It's the mistake, because you're one move ahead. The engine goes from about plus 0.5 to about minus 1.7.
You take the knight. Your pawn is on b3 now, two squares from the king.
White takes your knight, and hits your bishop. It looks like a fair trade.
It isn't. Pawn takes a2, with check. Your rook on a8 guards it, so the king can't take.
The king has two squares. The corner would have kept White in the game. But c1 looks safer, away from that pawn.
It becomes a queen, guarded by your rook, and that's checkmate on move eighteen. That small pawn on a6 was the whole opening, and it finished the game.

chapters.title: Your game plan
chapters.from: e4 c5 Nf3 d6 d4 cxd4 Nxd4 Nf6 Nc3 a6

beats.card: So how do you win with this?
beats.say: The opening is the easy part. Here's the whole plan in three lines.
One. Five fixed moves, ending in a6. Then wait and see where White's bishop goes.
Two. Against a bishop on e3, or a quiet one, play e5, and watch d5. Against a bishop on g5 or c4, play e6.

beats.play: f3 Be7 Qd2 O-O O-O-O Nbd7
beats.say: Three. Finish your jobs. If White's king goes long, run your a-pawn and b-pawn at it, and when your knight is hit, look to hit back before you retreat.
That's a good way to win quick games. It isn't magic. A careful White keeps a small edge, and then you have to think.
So do two things next. Drill these lines until your hands know them, then read the Najdorf plan for what to do when the punch doesn't land.
